text_raw: Bologna, 24 March, 1527, third hour of night.

text: I have not -writteii to your Lordships for two days, having been at Pianoro to review the troops.
text_raw:
I have not -writteii to your Lordships for two days, having
been at Pianoro to review the troops.

text: I returned here to-day, and found matters in the same condition in which I had left them ; for there is as yet nothing definite from the Pieramosca, although the Lord Lieutenant has written him every day, and has with that prudence which is necessary under such circum- stances urged him to bring matters to some definite conclusion.
text_raw:
I returned here to-day,
and found matters in the same condition in which I had left
them ; for there is as yet nothing definite from the Pieramosca,
although the Lord Lieutenant has written him every day, and
has with that prudence which is necessary under such circum-
stances urged him to bring matters to some definite conclusion.

text: The weather has been and continues bad, so that if the Span- iards have not scoured the country during the past two days it has been solely on that account.
text_raw:
The weather has been and continues bad, so that if the Span-
iards have not scoured the country during the past two days
it has been solely on that account.

text: Nevertheless, we liear that "war is resolved upon ; for we learn from those sources whence we have been in the habit of receiving news, that the enemy have changed their intention of coming into Tuscany by the Sasso, or by any other route equally convenient, because they are frightened by the bad roads and the weather ; and that they intend coming by way of Romagna, and entering Tuscany by the Marecchia.
text_raw:
Nevertheless, we liear that
"war is resolved upon ; for we learn from those sources whence
we have been in the habit of receiving news, that the enemy have
changed their intention of coming into Tuscany by the Sasso,
or by any other route equally convenient, because they are
frightened by the bad roads and the weather ; and that they
intend coming by way of Romagna, and entering Tuscany by
the Marecchia.

text: They purpose occupying some one of the most important towns on that road, and to be able to do so the more securely, they want to arrive there before the troops of the Church in the following manner.
text_raw:
They purpose occupying some one of the most
important towns on that road, and to be able to do so the more
securely, they want to arrive there before the troops of the
Church in the following manner.

text: They will make their first halt at Ponte a Reno, and in that way they hope to keep us qmet and in doubt, as they can take different routes from there and attempt different attacks.
text_raw:
They will make their first
halt at Ponte a Reno, and in that way they hope to keep us
qmet and in doubt, as they can take different routes from
there and attempt different attacks.

text: After that they will di- vide their forces, one portion remaining here and feigning an attack on this city, and the other part will turn below Bologna, placing itself half-way between Bologna and Imola.
text_raw:
After that they will di-
vide their forces, one portion remaining here and feigning an
attack on this city, and the other part will turn below Bologna,
placing itself half-way between Bologna and Imola.

text: They be- lieve that they can carry this plan out in security, as they believe that either division of their forces is stronger than we are all together, and that they can moreover unite their entire forces with perfect safety should it be necessary.
text_raw:
They be-
lieve that they can carry this plan out in security, as they
believe that either division of their forces is stronger than we
are all together, and that they can moreover unite their entire
forces with perfect safety should it be necessary.

text: And thus they count on being ahead of our troops, and finding the towns unprepared ; and after having taken one, they think the others will have to act according to their will.
text_raw:
And thus
they count on being ahead of our troops, and finding the towns
unprepared ; and after having taken one, they think the others
will have to act according to their will.

text: Our situation seems to me the same that it has been ever since we have been here ; that is, one day we hear that one thing has been resolved upon, and the next day we hear of another plan directly the ffeverse ; and therefore the one is as
text_raw:
Our situation seems to me the same that it has been ever
since we have been here ; that is, one day we hear that one
thing has been resolved upon, and the next day we hear of
another plan directly the ffeverse ; and therefore the one is as

text: much to be believed as the one that has been told and written before ; nor is there as yet any positive reason for apprehend- ing that the truce will not be concluded.
text_raw:
much to be believed as the one that has been told and written
before ; nor is there as yet any positive reason for apprehend-
ing that the truce will not be concluded.

text: Still, it is necessary promptly to come to some conclusion either for or against it, for many reasons, and mainly to enable us here to inspire the Venetians with confidence, and settle the minds of the French troops, so that we may not find ourselves left alone to bear the burden of this war.
text_raw:
Still, it is necessary
promptly to come to some conclusion either for or against it,
for many reasons, and mainly to enable us here to inspire the
Venetians with confidence, and settle the minds of the French
troops, so that we may not find ourselves left alone to bear the
burden of this war.

text: For as the truce, if concluded, will be our safety, so, on the contrary, if it is deferred or not concluded will it be our ruin.
text_raw:
For as the truce, if concluded, will be our
safety, so, on the contrary, if it is deferred or not concluded
will it be our ruin.

text: Nor do I believe that there is any one who thinks differently.
text_raw:
Nor do I believe that there is any one who
thinks differently.

text: But when Heaven intends to conceal its designs, it leads men to that point that they cannot adopt any definite plan for their safety.
text_raw:
But when Heaven intends to conceal its
designs, it leads men to that point that they cannot adopt any
definite plan for their safety.

text: I have nothing further to add, except to recommend myself to your Lordships, quce feliciores sint.
text_raw:
I have nothing further to add,
except to recommend myself to your Lordships, quce feliciores
sint.

text: I wrote to your Lordships day before yesterday.
text_raw: I wrote to your Lordships day before yesterday.

text: Since then we have the following respecting the truce.
text_raw:
Since then
we have the following respecting the truce.

text: Messer Giovanni del Yantaggio returned yesterday evening from the Spanish camp, where he had gone with the Fieramosca, and reports confusion and differences between the captains and the troops ; the latter do not want the truce, whilst the captains, and espe- cially the Captain-General, are in favor of it.
text_raw:
Messer Giovanni
del Yantaggio returned yesterday evening from the Spanish
camp, where he had gone with the Fieramosca, and reports
confusion and differences between the captains and the troops ;
the latter do not want the truce, whilst the captains, and espe-
cially the Captain-General, are in favor of it.

text: Messer Giovanni adds, that he came away from the camp partly because he did not like to remain there, and partly for the purpose of reporting the condition of things there.
text_raw:
Messer Giovanni
adds, that he came away from the camp partly because he did not
like to remain there, and partly for the purpose of reporting
the condition of things there.

text: This evening, after five o'clock, news came that the enemy had broken up and were marching to Ponte a Keno to effect the division there of which I gave notice to your Lordships in my last letter.
text_raw:
This evening, after five o'clock,
news came that the enemy had broken up and were marching
to Ponte a Keno to effect the division there of which I gave
notice to your Lordships in my last letter.

text: They have not yet started this morning, but we are told that they will certainly do so to-morrow morning, and that they intend to retrace their steps so as to enter Tuscany by the Garfagnana, for the rea- sons which I have already written to your Lordships.
text_raw:
They have not yet
started this morning, but we are told that they will certainly
do so to-morrow morning, and that they intend to retrace their
steps so as to enter Tuscany by the Garfagnana, for the rea-
sons which I have already written to your Lordships.

text: Thus we are in the greatest uncertainty as to what we ought to do.
text_raw:
Thus
we are in the greatest uncertainty as to what we ought to do.

text: To-day at about noon a trumpeter came with a letter from Mon- seigneur de Bourbon to the most illustrious Legate, telling him how greatly he had desired peace, and the efforts he had made to obtain the assent of the troops to the truce, but that he had not been able to satisfy them ; and telling him that he needed more money, but did not state the amount.
text_raw:
To-day at about noon a trumpeter came with a letter from Mon-
seigneur de Bourbon to the most illustrious Legate, telling him
how greatly he had desired peace, and the efforts he had made
to obtain the assent of the troops to the truce, but that he had
not been able to satisfy them ; and telling him that he needed
more money, but did not state the amount.

text: He therefore begged his Lordship not to be surprised if he saw the enemy start in the morning, as he was not able to prevent it ; and he suggests that it would be well to make everything known at Rome, so that the Viceroy and the Pope may satisfy the troops by new agreements, and that he will do the same.
text_raw:
He therefore
begged his Lordship not to be surprised if he saw the enemy
start in the morning, as he was not able to prevent it ; and he
suggests that it would be well to make everything known at
Rome, so that the Viceroy and the Pope may satisfy the troops
by new agreements, and that he will do the same.

text: Everybody therefore, Magnificent Signori, regards the truce as good as broken, and that nothing remains except to think of war, un- less, indeed, the Almighty should come to our aid by inspiring these men to be more humble.
text_raw:
Everybody
therefore, Magnificent Signori, regards the truce as good as
broken, and that nothing remains except to think of war, un-
less, indeed, the Almighty should come to our aid by inspiring
these men to be more humble.

text: For it seems that in the new negotiations that are being carried on, it is agreed to expend what money you have in the payment of these troops ; and then, if we wish them to agree to a truce, you would need to have, besides this present payment to the troops, at least one hundred thousand florins disposable in your purse.
text_raw:
For it seems that in the new
negotiations that are being carried on, it is agreed to expend
what money you have in the payment of these troops ; and
then, if we wish them to agree to a truce, you would need to
have, besides this present payment to the troops, at least one
hundred thousand florins disposable in your purse.

text: And as this cannot be, it is folly to waste time in making a bargain which we could not carry out afterwards for want of money.
text_raw:
And as
this cannot be, it is folly to waste time in making a bargain
which we could not carry out afterwards for want of money.

text: Let your Lordships therefore prepare for war, win back the Venetians, and make sure of them, so that their troops that have passed the Po will return to our assistance.
text_raw:
Let your Lordships therefore prepare for war, win back the
Venetians, and make sure of them, so that their troops that
have passed the Po will return to our assistance.

text: And bear in mind that inasmuch as tliis truce, if concluded, would have been our salvation, so it may in not being concluded and keep- ing us in suspense prove our ruin.
text_raw:
And bear in
mind that inasmuch as tliis truce, if concluded, would have
been our salvation, so it may in not being concluded and keep-
ing us in suspense prove our ruin.

text: The enemy's troops did not start, as in my letter of yesterday I reported they intended to do.
text_raw:
The enemy's troops did not start, as in my letter of yesterday
I reported they intended to do.

text: I believe the cause is the heavy rain and snow that has continued falling all night.
text_raw:
I believe the cause is the heavy
rain and snow that has continued falling all night.

text: We do not know, therefore, whether they will move to-morrow or not, but we do know that they maintain themselves here with the great-
text_raw:
We do not
know, therefore, whether they will move to-morrow or not, but
we do know that they maintain themselves here with the great-

text: est difficulty, so that it seems almost impossible for them to remain here ; and what ought to alarm them most is that they cannot better themselves by a change of encampment.
text_raw:
est difficulty, so that it seems almost impossible for them to
remain here ; and what ought to alarm them most is that they
cannot better themselves by a change of encampment.

text: If these difficulties were increased in any way by us, they would assuredly be destroyed ; but our own unfortunate position pre- vents our doing anything of the kind.
text_raw:
If
these difficulties were increased in any way by us, they would
assuredly be destroyed ; but our own unfortunate position pre-
vents our doing anything of the kind.

text: This causes the Lord Lieutenant the greatest anxiety ; he organizes and applies remedies wherever he can ; may it please the Almighty to enable him to do what is necessary to produce the desired effect!
text_raw:
This causes the Lord
Lieutenant the greatest anxiety ; he organizes and applies
remedies wherever he can ; may it please the Almighty to
enable him to do what is necessary to produce the desired
effect!

text: Nothing more is heard of the Fieramosca or of the truce ;
text_raw:
Nothing more is heard of the Fieramosca or of the
truce ;

text: I have therefore nothing further to tell you on that subject.
text_raw:
I have therefore nothing further to tell you on that
subject.

text: Every one has come to the conclusion that we have nothing to expect but war, since the perfidy of others prevented the success of a peace that would have been most useful and beneficial.
text_raw:
Every one has come to the conclusion that we have
nothing to expect but war, since the perfidy of others prevented
the success of a peace that would have been most useful and
beneficial.

text: There is no occasion, therefore, to delay resolving upon war ; it should be done at once, so as to show to everybody that it is idle to think any more of peace.
text_raw:
There is no occasion, therefore, to delay resolving
upon war ; it should be done at once, so as to show to
everybody that it is idle to think any more of peace.

text: But we must act so that the Venetians and the king of France shall have no fear of our concluding any peace without their consent.
text_raw:
But
we must act so that the Venetians and the king of France
shall have no fear of our concluding any peace without their
consent.

text: And if this be done, and you succeed promptly in winning back the Venetians so that they come effectually to our assistance, then the delays which the storm has caused to the enemy will prove an advantage to us, inasmuch as it will have given us time enough for our forces to be sufficiently united to hold them in check.
text_raw:
And if this be done, and you succeed promptly in
winning back the Venetians so that they come effectually to our
assistance, then the delays which the storm has caused to the
enemy will prove an advantage to us, inasmuch as it will have
given us time enough for our forces to be sufficiently united to
hold them in check.

text: For your Lordships will see that it was fifteen days ago to-day that they decided to pass, but have not yet been able to do it ; so that we may reasonably hope that the same causes may keep them fifteen days more, if not here where they are, at least this side of the mountains.
text_raw:
For your Lordships will see that it was
fifteen days ago to-day that they decided to pass, but have not
yet been able to do it ; so that we may reasonably hope that
the same causes may keep them fifteen days more, if not here
where they are, at least this side of the mountains.

text: But it be- hooves us, as I have said, to employ this time well, otherwise our ruin will only liave been postponed, and will be the greater, the same as bodies that have been enfeebled by long disease are less able to support it than they were in its beginning.
text_raw:
But it be-
hooves us, as I have said, to employ this time well, otherwise
our ruin will only liave been postponed, and will be the greater,
the same as bodies that have been enfeebled by long disease
are less able to support it than they were in its beginning.

text: I have not -written you for three days because so soon as the enemy moved from San Giovanni the Lord Lieutenant sent me here to provide quarters for the troops that are to arrive.
text_raw:
I have not -written you for three days because so soon as
the enemy moved from San Giovanni the Lord Lieutenant sent
me here to provide quarters for the troops that are to arrive.

text: Your Lordships will have learned from his letters that the enemy encamped day before yesterday at Ponte a Reno, but made no movement yesterday.
text_raw:
Your Lordships will have learned from his letters that the
enemy encamped day before yesterday at Ponte a Reno, but
made no movement yesterday.

text: The Lord President with the Marquis of Saluzzo and the Count Cajazzo, and all the rest of our troops, came here ; and there remain in Bologna only the infantry of the Signor Giovanni, and those that are ordinarily stationed there.
text_raw:
The Lord President with the
Marquis of Saluzzo and the Count Cajazzo, and all the rest of
our troops, came here ; and there remain in Bologna only the
infantry of the Signor Giovanni, and those that are ordinarily
stationed there.

text: We have not yet heard to-day that the enemy has moved ; and it is supposed either that they have not moved, or that they have made but little progress, so that it will take more than two days' march for them to arrive here.
text_raw:
We have not yet heard to-day that the enemy
has moved ; and it is supposed either that they have not
moved, or that they have made but little progress, so that it
will take more than two days' march for them to arrive here.

text: If we hear of his coming here, we shall leave fifteen himdred men here.
text_raw:
If we hear of his coming here, we shall leave fifteen himdred
men here.

text: The Count Cajazzo has been sent with all his infan- try to Ravenna, and thus we shall go on aiding and providing, so as to prevent the enemy from taking any important place.
And if he does succeed in doing this, he will certainly be ruined ; or he will be obliged to accept the truce that has been made.
text_raw:
And if he does succeed in doing this, he will certainly be
ruined ; or he will be obliged to accept the truce that has been
made.

text: But if our evil fortune should prevent this truce from being definitely concluded, then it will be better to avoid it by continuing the war, than to show that we desire it eagerly.
text_raw:
But if our evil fortune should prevent this truce from
being definitely concluded, then it will be better to avoid it by
continuing the war, than to show that we desire it eagerly.

text: For the enemy have manifested their ill feeling so openly to- wards Italy, and more especially towards Florence, which they regard as their prey, that until they are undeceived upon that point they will look upon any arrangement as unreasonable, un- less they are moved by the authority of the Viceroy in some way that I do not understand.
text_raw:
For the enemy have manifested their ill feeling so openly to-
wards Italy, and more especially towards Florence, which they
regard as their prey, that until they are undeceived upon that
point they will look upon any arrangement as unreasonable, un-
less they are moved by the authority of the Viceroy in some
way that I do not understand.

text: For it is believed that the latter, the Fieramosca, and the Marchese del Guasto act most willingly in this matter ; for he has gone expressly to Rome, and the Fie- ramosca, according to what he writes, has done the impossible on his part:
text_raw:
For it is believed that the latter,
the Fieramosca, and the Marchese del Guasto act most willingly
in this matter ; for he has gone expressly to Rome, and the Fie-
ramosca, according to what he writes, has done the impossible
on his part:

text: And as to the Marchese, it is reported that, hav- ing asked for a safe-conduct to go to Naples through Romagna, and not having started yet, he has renewed his request, beg- ging that it might be granted to him with the alternative to go through Florence and Rome, as he wished to speak with the Pope and discuss these matters with him ; he complains much
text_raw:
And as to the Marchese, it is reported that, hav-
ing asked for a safe-conduct to go to Naples through Romagna,
and not having started yet, he has renewed his request, beg-
ging that it might be granted to him with the alternative to go
through Florence and Rome, as he wished to speak with the
Pope and discuss these matters with him ; he complains much

text: of the wickedness of those who disturb this peace.
text_raw: of the wickedness of those who disturb this peace.

text: All this is very well, and may help us to get our troops together if the war is not given up ; otherwise no reasonable agreement is to be hoped for.
text_raw:
All this is
very well, and may help us to get our troops together if the
war is not given up ; otherwise no reasonable agreement is to
be hoped for.

text: For what sort of an arrangement can you ex- pect from an enemy, who, despite of having the Alps between you and himself, and with the number of troops which you have on foot, still asks one hundred thousand florins of you within the space of three days, and one hundred and fifty thousand within ten days ?
text_raw:
For what sort of an arrangement can you ex-
pect from an enemy, who, despite of having the Alps between
you and himself, and with the number of troops which you
have on foot, still asks one hundred thousand florins of you
within the space of three days, and one hundred and fifty
thousand within ten days ?

text: When he gets to Florence tlie first thing he will ask of you will be all the movable property you possess.
text_raw:
When he gets to Florence tlie first
thing he will ask of you will be all the movable property you
possess.

text: For without doubt (would it were not so !) the only inducement they have for advancing is the hope of pillaging your city.
text_raw:
For without doubt (would it were not so !) the only
inducement they have for advancing is the hope of pillaging
your city.

text: And there is no other way of escaping these evils but to undeceive the enemy as to your ability to resist him ; and if this is to be done, then it is better to do it in the moun- tains than within our city walls, and to employ all the forces we have to keep him there.
text_raw:
And there is no other way of escaping these evils
but to undeceive the enemy as to your ability to resist him ;
and if this is to be done, then it is better to do it in the moun-
tains than within our city walls, and to employ all the forces
we have to keep him there.

text: For if the enemy is detained in the mountains but a short time he will have to disband, as we learn from reliable quarters that if they do not succeed within the present month in taking some one of the large places, in which they will not succeed unless the places are abandoned, then they must of necessity succumb.
text_raw:
For if the enemy is detained in
the mountains but a short time he will have to disband, as we
learn from reliable quarters that if they do not succeed within
the present month in taking some one of the large places, in
which they will not succeed unless the places are abandoned,
then they must of necessity succumb.

text: And even if you should not succeed in defending yourselves on the other side or within the mountains, there will be nothing to prevent you from bring- ing the forces which you have there over to this side.
text_raw:
And even if you should
not succeed in defending yourselves on the other side or within
the mountains, there will be nothing to prevent you from bring-
ing the forces which you have there over to this side.

text: For I remember in the war with Pisa, that the Pisans, wearied by its long duration, began to discuss amongst themselves whether they ought not to make terms with you.
text_raw:
For I
remember in the war with Pisa, that the Pisans, wearied by its
long duration, began to discuss amongst themselves whether
they ought not to make terms with you.

text: Pandolfo Petrucci, anticipating such an attempt, sent Messer Antonio da Venafro to dissuade them from it.
text_raw:
Pandolfo Petrucci,
anticipating such an attempt, sent Messer Antonio da Venafro
to dissuade them from it.

text: Messer Antonio addressed them in public meeting, and after many other things said to them, " that they had passed a very tempestuous sea, and wanted now " to drown themselves in a well." I do not mention this be- cause I think that Florence is about to abandon herself to de- spair, but to give you certain hope of safety provided you are willing rather to spend ten florins to secure your safety, than forty that would serve to enslave and ruin you.
text_raw:
Messer Antonio addressed them in
public meeting, and after many other things said to them,
" that they had passed a very tempestuous sea, and wanted now
" to drown themselves in a well." I do not mention this be-
cause I think that Florence is about to abandon herself to de-
spair, but to give you certain hope of safety provided you are
willing rather to spend ten florins to secure your safety, than
forty that would serve to enslave and ruin you.

text: I recommend myself to your Lordships, quoe bene valecmt.
text_raw:
I recommend
myself to your Lordships, quoe bene valecmt.

text: My previous letters will have informed you of all that has taken place here up till now.
text_raw:
My previous letters will have informed you of all that has
taken place here up till now.

text: By the present you will learn that the enemy did not leave his encampment of the night before between Imola and Paenza, whence we greatly feared they would take the road to Tuscany.
text_raw:
By the present you will learn
that the enemy did not leave his encampment of the night
before between Imola and Paenza, whence we greatly feared
they would take the road to Tuscany.

text: They sent a trumpeter to Paenza on behalf of Monseigneur de Bourbon, demanding in his name three things.
text_raw:
They sent a trumpeter
to Paenza on behalf of Monseigneur de Bourbon, demanding in
his name three things.

text: The first was to grant free passage to his troops close under the walls of the place ; the second, to supply him witli provisions on being paid for them in cash ; and the third was to receive his sick people within their town so that they might be cured there.
text_raw:
The first was to grant free passage to
his troops close under the walls of the place ; the second, to
supply him witli provisions on being paid for them in cash ;
and the third was to receive his sick people within their town
so that they might be cured there.

text: All three of these demands were refused, and although the inhabitants were at first a little displeased at receiving our troops into garrison, yet they after- wards received them, and showed themselves more courageous and disposed to defend themselves.
text_raw:
All three of these demands
were refused, and although the inhabitants were at first a little
displeased at receiving our troops into garrison, yet they after-
wards received them, and showed themselves more courageous
and disposed to defend themselves.

text: This morning, however, the enemy's army approached within gunshot of Paenza, and then turned off to the left, taking the lower road to Ravenna ; so that we feel sure for the moment that they will not enter Tuscany.
text_raw:
This morning, however,
the enemy's army approached within gunshot of Paenza, and
then turned off to the left, taking the lower road to Ravenna ;
so that we feel sure for the moment that they will not enter
Tuscany.

text: We are also almost certain for the present that they will not attempt to take any of the places in Romagna ; and as we have supplied Paenza, Imola, and Purli with provisions, so we shall equally supply Ravenna, Cesena, and Rimini.
text_raw:
We are also almost certain for the present that they
will not attempt to take any of the places in Romagna ; and
as we have supplied Paenza, Imola, and Purli with provisions,
so we shall equally supply Ravenna, Cesena, and Rimini.

text: And those places that cannot now be supplied by land will be supplied by sea, so that they can remain perfectly safe, unless something quite unexpected should happen.
text_raw:
And those places that cannot now be supplied by land will be
supplied by sea, so that they can remain perfectly safe, unless
something quite unexpected should happen.

text: The Count Guide, who was with his troops at Modena, and the infantry of the Signer Giovanni, which had been left at Bologna, must, at the moment of my writing, have arrived at Imola.
text_raw:
The Count Guide, who was with his troops at Modena, and
the infantry of the Signer Giovanni, which had been left at
Bologna, must, at the moment of my writing, have arrived at
Imola.

text: We are here at Purli with the Swiss and the Prench troops ; and they fight with much reluctance.
text_raw:
We are here at Purli with the Swiss and the Prench
troops ; and they fight with much reluctance.

text: The command- ers of these troops, so soon as they are separated from the Lord Lieutenant, carry out the plans agreed upon either very slowly or very badly.
text_raw:
The command-
ers of these troops, so soon as they are separated from the
Lord Lieutenant, carry out the plans agreed upon either very
slowly or very badly.

text: These soldiers are insupportable, and the inhabitants of the country are so afraid of them that they receive them most unwillingly.
text_raw:
These soldiers are insupportable, and
the inhabitants of the country are so afraid of them that they
receive them most unwillingly.

text: The troops of the League move very slowly, as they have no confidence in the truce, and the reported coming of the Viceroy would have disaffected
text_raw:
The troops of the League
move very slowly, as they have no confidence in the truce, and
the reported coming of the Viceroy would have disaffected

text: them entirely if the Lord Lieutenant had not represented to them that it amounted to nothing.
text_raw:

text: The Duke Valentino had returned from Lombardy, where he had gone to exculpate himself to King Louis XII. of Prance from the many calumnies that had been told of him on account of the revolt of Arezzo and other places in the Val di Chiana.

text: In June last the Emperor held a Diet at Constanz of all the princes of Germany, to provide for his passage into Italy, for the purpose of being crowned.

text: The French are by nature more ferocious than vigorous and adroit ; and if you can resist the fury of their first onset, you will find them so depressed and so entirely discouraged, that they become cowardly like women.

text: By the extent of her territory and the advantages derived from her large rivers, France is very productive and opulent ; but the abundant productions of the soil, as well as manual labor, have little or no value, owing to the scarcity of money amongst the people, who can scarcely get enough together to pay their dues to the lord proprietor, although tlie amounts are but very small.
text_raw:
By the extent of her territory and the advantages derived
from her large rivers, France is very productive and opulent ;
but the abundant productions of the soil, as well as manual
labor, have little or no value, owing to the scarcity of money
amongst the people, who can scarcely get enough together to
pay their dues to the lord proprietor, although tlie amounts
are but very small.

text: This arises from their not having an out- let for the productions of the soil, for every man gathers enough to sell some ; so that if in any one place a man wanted to sell a bushel of grain, he would not find a purchaser, everybody having grain to sell.
text_raw:
This arises from their not having an out-
let for the productions of the soil, for every man gathers enough
to sell some ; so that if in any one place a man wanted to sell

text: And of the money which the gentlemen draw from their tenants, they spend nothing except for their clothing; for they have cattle enough to give them meat, innu- merable fowls, lakes full of fish, and parks with an abundance of every variety of game ; and thus almost every gentleman lives upon his estates.
text_raw:
And of the money which the gentlemen

clothing; for they have cattle enough to give them meat, innu-

text: In this way all the money accumulates in the hands of the proprietors, and their wealth is accordingly great ; whilst the people, when they have a florin, deem them- selves rich.

text: And as they have abundant supplies of all the necessaries of life, all the revenues and moneys that come into their hands never leave them again, according to the avaricious nature of prelates and churchmen ; and all the money that is col- lected by the chapters and colleges of the Church is spent for silver, jewels, and costly church ornaments.

text: In the council for the direction and management of the af- fairs of the crown and the state of France, the prelates always constitute the majority ; the other lords care nothing about this, for they know that the execution of the decisions always devolves upon them ; and thus both are satisfied, the first with the direction, and the others with the execution ; although at times old and experienced officers are called into the council, when military matters have to be discussed and decided, so that they may guide the prelates, who have no practical ex- perience in these matters.

text: In virtue of a certain pragmatic sanction * obtained long ago from the Popes, all the Church benefices of France are be- stowed by their colleges ; so that, in case of the death of a bishop or an archbishop, the canons of the Church meet and confer the benefice upon the individual amongst themselves who seems to them to merit it most.
text_raw:

bishop or an archbishop, the canons of the Church meet and
confer the benefice upon the individual amongst themselves

text: It happens not unfre- quently that this gives rise to dissensions amongst them, for there are always some who are favored on account of their riches, and others for their virtues and good works.

text: And if the king ever attempts to disparage this pragmatic sanction by appoint- ing a bishop of his own choice, he would have to employ force to put him in possession, which the canons would refuse him ; and if they had to yield to this force, they would abide the death of the king to expel that bishop from his see, and give it to the one elected by themselves.

text: France fears the English, because she remembers the incur- sions and devastations by the latter in the realm ; so that the very name of English is a terror to the people, who do not bear in mind that France is nowadays in a very different position from what she was in those unhappy times.
text_raw:
France fears the English, because she remembers the incur-

very name of English is a terror to the people, who do not bear
in mind that France is nowadays in a very different position
from what she was in those unhappy times.

text: For she is armed, experienced in war, and united, and has possession of those very provinces which served the English as a basis for their operations, such as the duchies of Brittany and of Burgundy.

text: Moreover, the English are no longer disciplined, for it is a long while since they have had a war, so that none of the people now living have ever seen an enemy's face ; and then there is no one save the Archduke who would be willing to see them on the Continent.
text_raw:
Moreover, the English are no longer disciplined, for it is a long

text: The French would be much afraid of the Spaniards on ac- count of their sagacity and vigilance.

text: But every time that the king of Spain would attack France, he would have to do it at great disadvantage ; for from that point in his kingdom from which his troops would have to start to the foot of the Pyre- nees which stretch into France, the distance is so great and the country so sterile that if the French make a stand at the entrance of the Pyrenees by way of Perpignan or Guienne, the enemy's army would be disorganized, if not from want of reinforcements, at least from the difficulty of obtaining pro- visions, which wou^d have to be brought from a great distance.

text: For the country which has to be traversed is uninhabited on account of its sterility, and those who do inhabit it have scarcely enough to sustain their own existence.
text_raw:

text: Nothing is to be apprehended by the French of the Flemish, whose country is so cold that they cannot raise sufficient pro- visions, and particularly grain and wine, which they have to procure from Burgundy, Picardy, and some other provinces of France.

factures, as well as other merchandise, at the French fairs;

text: The Swiss are much feared by the French, owing to their close proximity, and the facility with which they can make sudden and unexpected attacks, against which, owing to their rapidity, it is impossible to provide in time.
text_raw:
The Swiss are much feared by the French, owing to their

text: These incursions of the Swiss, however, are mere predatory raids ; for as they have neither artillery nor horses, and as the strong places which the French possess near the frontier are well supplied with munitions, the Swiss are not able to make much progress.
text_raw:
These incursions
of the Swiss, however, are mere predatory raids ; for as they

text: And then the nature of the Swiss is better suited to battles in the open field than to sieges or to the defence of places.
text_raw:
And then the nature of the Swiss is better suited to battles in

text: But the French of the frontier do not like to come to an open hand- to-hand fight with the Swiss, for they have no good infantry that can withstand the Swiss, and the men-at-arms without infantry do not amount to much.

But
the French of the frontier do not like to come to an open hand-

text: The country, moreover, is so formed that lances and other mounted men can but illy manoeu- vre there, whilst the Swiss go most unwillingly far from their frontiers to reach level ground; for they would leave behind them strong places well supplied with everything, as stated above.
text_raw:

formed that lances and other mounted men can but illy manoeu-
vre there, whilst the Swiss go most unwillingly far from their

text: However, France has nothing to fear from the side of Italy, for the reasons above stated, and because there is not in all Italy a prince capable of assaulting France, and Italy herseK is not united, as she was in the time of the Romans.

text: On the south side, Prance is sufficiently protected by the Mediterranean, in the ports of which there are always vessels enough, belonging to the king of Prance or other proprietors, to be able to defend that part of the kingdom from any unex- pected attack.

pected attack.

text: Against a premeditated attack there is always time to prepare, for whoever contemplates it needs time to make the necessary preparations and arrangements, and this will quickly become known to everybody.
